name: Compare delivery speed and spread
before_text: Run Supplier A. Read its mean, spread and delivery-time histogram.
change: Change SUPPLIER from A to B. Keep the same completed orders and date range.
observe: Compare the histograms using their fixed axes and the two supplier rows.
questions: Which supplier is faster on average, and which has a wider spread of delivery times?
A buyer says, “B arrives faster, so its timing is more predictable.” Do both parts follow from these outputs?
Explain the difference between speed and consistency to the buyer using one value for each.
answers: B is faster: 9.0 days on average versus 10.3 for A. B has wider spread: standard deviation 2.47 days versus 0.91 for A.
Only the speed claim is supported. B ranges from 5 to 13 days while A ranges from 9 to 12. The larger spread makes B less consistent in this case.
“B averages 9.0 days, but its timing varies more: spread is 2.47 days versus A’s 0.91. We should discuss both average speed and consistency when reviewing delivery performance.”

name: Read delivery performance against a target
before_text: Use the internal target of 10 days. Read the target percentage and promised-date OTD.
change: Change TARGET_DAYS from 10 to 12. Original promises and actual receipts stay fixed.
observe: Compare the internal-target bars with the promised-date bars.
questions: Which percentages change when the internal target moves from 10 to 12 days?
The reported target percentage improves. Have any suppliers actually delivered sooner?
A colleague wants to tell management that delivery performance improved. Explain what this run really changed.
answers: Within-target percentages change: A 60% to 100%, B 70% to 90%, C 50% to 70%. Promised-date OTD stays A 90%, B 90%, C 50%.
No receipt dates change. More existing deliveries fit a more generous internal target.
“We changed the internal target from 10 to 12 days, so more orders meet it. Delivery dates and performance against the original promised dates have not changed.”

name: Compare two quality measures
before_text: Read the percentage of completed orders containing any defective unit.
change: Change QUALITY_VIEW from orders to units.
observe: Read both denominators in the table and compare the A/B ranking. The chart scale changes with the measure.
questions: Compare A and B: which has fewer flagged orders, and which has the lower defective-unit percentage?
Why can B have fewer flagged orders but a larger defective-unit percentage? Use the counts in the table.
A manager calls B “better quality” using only flagged orders. Explain what the second measure adds.
answers: B has 6/60 flagged orders (10%) versus A’s 12/60 (20%). A has the lower defective-unit percentage: 72/29,940 = 0.2405%, versus B’s 180/29,980 = 0.6004%.
B has fewer affected orders, but more defective units within those affected orders. Order incidence and the proportion of units defective answer different questions.
“B has quality incidents on fewer orders, but those incidents contain more defective units overall. We should report both the frequency of affected orders and the defective-unit percentage.”

name: Compare purchase price and recorded cost
before_text: Compare purchase prices for the same VALVE20 component in EUR per piece.
change: Change COST_BASIS from purchase to recorded.
observe: Compare purchase-only and recorded procurement cost per received unit.
questions: Which supplier has the lowest purchase price? Which has the lowest recorded cost per received unit?
What included costs explain why the ranking changes?
A colleague says the cheapest quoted supplier must cost the least overall. Explain what the cost table supports and one cost it still leaves out.
answers: A has the lowest purchase price at EUR 9.00. B has the lowest recorded cost at EUR 10.348/unit, versus A 10.519 and C 10.396.
Recorded cost adds freight, inspection and rework. A’s low price is offset by higher freight and inspection costs in this synthetic case.

“A has the lowest purchase price, while B has the lowest cost across the recorded categories. We have not included downtime, financing, administration or later lifecycle costs, so this is not a complete total-cost-of-ownership comparison.”

name: Screen suppliers and check capacity
before_text: Apply the 1.0% defective-unit ceiling, Approved status and at least 85% promised-date OTD. July need is 9,000 units.
change: Change MAX_DEFECTIVE_PCT from 1.0 to 0.5. Keep all other rules and capacity figures fixed.
observe: Read each pass/fail column, the eligible suppliers and total available July capacity.
questions: Which suppliers qualify in each run, and what happens to capacity relative to the July requirement?
Did the stricter quality ceiling change supplier quality or the buyer’s acceptance rule?
Write a two-sentence follow-up for procurement: explain why B drops out, what to review with B, and why the remaining shortlist cannot cover July on its own.
answers: At 1.0%, A and B qualify with 14,000 units of combined capacity. At 0.5%, only A qualifies with 8,000 units, leaving a 1,000-unit gap against July’s 9,000-unit requirement. C fails qualification, delivery and quality in both runs.
Only the acceptance rule changes. B remains at 0.6004% defective units. Historical quality and available capacity are unchanged.

“B exceeds the stricter 0.5% ceiling, so procurement should review the defect records, agree a corrective action and track its defective-unit percentage. A alone offers 8,000 units against a need of 9,000, so the buyer must resolve the 1,000-unit gap before committing the sourcing plan.”
